patho-injury:response.q: Which outcome follows a stress that exceeds the cell's adaptive capacity but is mild and brief?
patho-injury:response.e: Mild, short injury can recover when the stress is removed.

patho-injury:response.q: Morphologic changes of cell death on light microscopy appear:
A 45-year-old man dies suddenly 15 minutes after the onset of crushing chest pain. Autopsy light microscopy of the left ventricle is most likely to show:
patho-injury:response.e: Biochemical death precedes visible light-microscopic change by hours.

patho-injury:adapt.q: Enlargement of the heart in long-standing hypertension is mainly:
patho-injury:adapt.e: Cardiomyocytes have limited ability to divide.

patho-injury:adapt.q: Barrett esophagus is an example of:
patho-injury:adapt.e: Squamous → columnar (intestinal) metaplasia; adaptation to acid reflux; may progress to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.

patho-injury:adapt.q: A 58-year-old smoker has a bronchial biopsy showing stratified squamous epithelium in place of ciliated columnar cells, with orderly maturation. If he continues smoking, the main risk is progression to:
patho-injury:adapt.e: Persistent stress can push metaplasia to dysplasia and carcinoma; stopping smoking can reverse it.

patho-injury:injury.q: A hallmark of reversible injury on electron microscopy:
o: Membrane blebs and loss of microvilli
patho-injury:injury.e: Large amorphous densities in mitochondria indicate irreversible injury; small ones can occur in reversible injury.

patho-injury:injury.q: Typical progression of nuclear changes in necrosis (as taught in First Aid):
Hepatocytes from a patient with heavy alcohol use show large cytoplasmic lipid vacuoles but intact membranes and normal nuclei. This change is best described as:
patho-injury:injury.e: Fatty change is a classic manifestation of reversible injury.

patho-injury:apoptosis.q: Which feature distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?
o: Leakage of cell enzymes into serum
patho-injury:apoptosis.e: Apoptotic bodies are cleared by phagocytes.

patho-injury:apoptosis.q: Cytochrome c release from mitochondria activates:
patho-injury:apoptosis.e: Intrinsic pathway; regulated by BCL-2 family.

patho-injury:apoptosis.q: A 9-year-old boy has massive lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly with many double-negative (CD4⁻CD8⁻) T cells and autoimmune cytopenias. The defect most likely involves:
patho-injury:apoptosis.e: Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome results from defective Fas-mediated deletion of lymphocytes.

patho-injury:necrosis.q: A brain infarct shows which pattern of necrosis?
patho-injury:necrosis.e: The brain liquefies after ischemic death (thought to reflect abundant lysosomal enzymes and little supporting matrix).

patho-injury:necrosis.q: Chalky white deposits in peripancreatic fat during acute pancreatitis represent:
patho-injury:necrosis.e: Lipases release fatty acids that bind calcium (saponification).

patho-injury:necrosis.q: A 70-year-old man has a stroke. Six weeks later the infarcted region is cystic and filled with fluid and macrophages. The original pattern of necrosis was:
patho-injury:necrosis.e: Brain infarcts liquefy and leave a cyst.

patho-injury:ischemia.q: Which liver zone is most sensitive to ischemia?
Cellular swelling in early ischemia results from:
patho-injury:ischemia.e: Na⁺ and water enter the cell.

patho-injury:ischemia.q: After an episode of profound hypotension, a patient develops jaundice and very high AST/ALT. Liver biopsy would show necrosis most prominent in:
patho-injury:ischemia.e: Zone 3 has the lowest oxygen supply; this is ischemic hepatitis.

patho-injury:infarct.e: Dual supply, loose tissue or venous occlusion.

patho-injury:infarct.q: A pale infarct is typical of:
A 30-year-old man has sudden severe testicular pain. Surgery 8 hours later finds a dark, congested, swollen testis. The infarct is red because:
o: It has an end-arterial blood supply
patho-injury:infarct.e: Torsion first occludes the thin-walled veins while arterial blood still enters, so blood collects in the tissue.

patho-injury:ros.q: The most reactive and damaging free radical:
patho-injury:ros.e: Generated by the Fenton reaction and radiation.

patho-injury:ros.q: Which enzyme converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide?
patho-injury:ros.e: Catalase and glutathione peroxidase then remove H₂O₂.

patho-injury:ros.q: A 52-year-old man with bronze skin, diabetes and cirrhosis has very high ferritin. Iron damages his tissues mainly by:
patho-injury:ros.e: Fe²⁺ converts H₂O₂ to •OH, causing lipid peroxidation; this is hereditary hemochromatosis.

patho-injury:radiation.q: Ionizing radiation damages cells mainly by:
patho-injury:radiation.e: Directly and via hydroxyl radicals from radiolysis of water. Rapidly dividing tissues are most sensitive.

patho-injury:radiation.q: Ten days after accidental whole-body radiation exposure, a worker has bloody diarrhea, fever and neutropenia. The tissues involved are injured first because they:
patho-injury:radiation.e: Rapidly dividing marrow and GI crypt cells are most radiosensitive.

patho-injury:calcif.e: Also meningioma, serous ovarian carcinoma and mesothelioma.

patho-injury:calcif.q: A 64-year-old woman with long-standing CKD (phosphate high, PTH high) has calcium deposits in otherwise normal lung alveolar walls. This is:
patho-injury:calcif.e: Deposition in normal tissue driven by abnormal calcium–phosphate levels.

patho-injury:amyloid.q: Amyloidosis in a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is most likely:
patho-injury:amyloid.e: Secondary to chronic inflammation; kidneys commonly involved.

patho-injury:amyloid.q: A 66-year-old man has nephrotic syndrome, an enlarged tongue and bruising around the eyes. Serum free λ light chains are high. The most appropriate first step to confirm the diagnosis is:
patho-injury:amyloid.e: Fat aspirate with Congo red stain is easy and usually positive in systemic AL amyloidosis; typing follows.

patho-injury:accum.q: The 'wear-and-tear' pigment seen in aging hearts is:
Hepatic steatosis is a manifestation of:
patho-injury:accum.e: Triglyceride accumulation; causes: alcohol, obesity, diabetes.

patho-injury:accum.q: A liver biopsy from a patient who received many blood transfusions shows golden-brown granules that turn blue with Prussian blue stain. The pigment is:
patho-injury:accum.e: Iron storage pigment; transfusion causes secondary iron overload.

patho-injury:mech.q: Increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ injures cells by:
patho-injury:mech.e: Phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases and ATPases. Also opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore.

patho-injury:mech.q: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER triggers:
patho-injury:mech.e: Chaperones up, translation down; apoptosis if overwhelmed.

patho-injury:mech.q: In a cell exposed to a toxin, cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises sharply. Which consequence follows directly?
patho-injury:mech.e: Calcium activates destructive enzymes and opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore.

patho-injury:otherdeath.e: Caspase-1 releases IL-1β; death of infected cells with fever-inducing IL-1.

patho-injury:otherdeath.q: Macrophages infected with Salmonella die and release large amounts of IL-1β. This form of death is:
patho-injury:otherdeath.e: Inflammasome → caspase-1 → IL-1β with cell death.

patho-injury:aging.e: Stem and cancer cells express telomerase.

patho-injury:aging.q: Werner syndrome (premature aging) results from a defect in:
A 30-year-old woman has gray hair, cataracts, skin atrophy and early atherosclerosis. Her disease most likely involves a defective:

title.th: เคสใหญ่: เจ็บหน้าอกตอนเช้า
title.en: Boss case: Crushing chest pain at dawn

boss.case: A 61-year-old man with diabetes and smoking history has 2 hours of crushing chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in V1–V4 and troponin is rising. Coronary flow is restored by PCI 5 hours after onset. He dies of an arrhythmia on day 3, and autopsy examines the anterior left ventricle.

qs.q: The dominant pattern of cell death in the infarcted myocardium:
qs.e: Ischemia of solid organs (except brain) causes coagulative necrosis.

qs.q: The earliest biochemical event in the ischemic myocyte:
qs.e: ↓ Oxidative phosphorylation → ATP depletion; ATP falls within minutes; morphology lags behind.

o: Plasma membrane damage of necrotic cells
qs.e: Leakage of intracellular proteins marks irreversible injury.

qs.q: After PCI, further injury from restored flow is mainly due to:
o: Reactive oxygen species and Ca²⁺ overload
qs.e: Ischemia–reperfusion injury: ROS and Ca²⁺ overload, plus leukocyte and complement activation.

qs.q: Which region of the heart is most vulnerable to ischemia?
qs.e: Farthest from the epicardial coronary supply.

qs.q: If he had survived for months, calcium deposits in the scar would be:
qs.e: Calcium deposits in dead tissue with normal serum calcium.

title.th: ไข้ ไอเรื้อรัง น้ำหนักลด
title.en: Chronic cough, fever and weight loss

stem.th: ชาย 45 ปี ไอมา 3 เดือน ไข้ต่ำๆ ตอนเย็น เหงื่อออกกลางคืน น้ำหนักลด 6 kg
stem.en: A 45-year-old man has 3 months of cough, evening fevers, night sweats and 6-kg weight loss.

steps.q: The lung lesion shows which type of necrosis?

info.th: CXR: cavity ที่ upper lobe ขวา · sputum AFB +
info.en: CXR: right upper lobe cavity · sputum acid-fast bacilli positive

steps.q: Old healed granulomas in his hilar nodes later show calcium with normal serum calcium. This is:
Chronic infection most likely caused deposition of:
steps.e: Chronic inflammation drives serum amyloid A.

info.th: หลายปีต่อมา มีขาบวม โปรตีนรั่วในปัสสาวะ
info.en: Years later he develops leg edema and nephrotic-range proteinuria

clues: 62-year-old man with leg swelling and fatigue
Months of easy bruising around the eyes after coughing
Enlarged tongue, hepatomegaly, ankle edema
Albumin 2.4 g/dL, serum free λ light chains very high
Urine protein 6 g/day · ECG low voltage
Fat pad biopsy: Congo red apple-green birefringence
dx.e: Light-chain amyloid from a plasma cell clone; heart and kidney involvement drive prognosis.

clues: 58-year-old woman with worsening leg edema
Rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years, poorly controlled
Deformed hands, hepatosplenomegaly
Albumin 2.2 g/dL, CRP persistently high, no monoclonal protein
Urine protein 5 g/day, bland sediment
Kidney biopsy: Congo red-positive deposits that stain for serum amyloid A
dx.e: Chronic inflammation drives serum amyloid A production; treat the underlying disease.

clues: 82-year-old man with exertional breathlessness
Bilateral carpal tunnel surgery years ago
Raised JVP, ankle edema, BP low-normal
NT-proBNP high, troponin mildly elevated, no monoclonal protein
ECG voltage low for the wall thickness on echo
Technetium pyrophosphate scan: strong cardiac uptake
dx.e: Wild-type transthyretin deposits in the heart of older men; restrictive cardiomyopathy.

clues: 50-year-old man with fatigue and joint pain
New diabetes; reduced libido
Bronze skin, hepatomegaly, 2nd–3rd MCP arthropathy
Ferritin 2,400 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 85%
HFE gene: C282Y homozygous
Liver biopsy: hemosiderin, Prussian blue positive
dx.e: Iron overload damages tissues via free radicals (Fenton reaction); treat with phlebotomy.
